title: Write texts on relevant topics in X

lessons.title: Planning what you write
lessons.html:
Planning what you write

This unit is about writing short texts in your chosen language (shown as X in the title, for example isiZulu, Sesotho, Afrikaans or English). At work in horticulture you write notes, messages, reports, lists, forms and short letters. Good writing saves time and prevents mistakes.

Before you write, ask four questions

  1. Who will read it? Your supervisor, a co-worker, a client, the office?
  2. Why am I writing? To give information, ask for something, report a problem, or say thank you?
  3. What must I say? List the main points.
  4. What kind of text is it? A note, a form, a report, an email, a letter?

Kinds of texts at work

TextExample in horticulture
Message or noteTelling the next shift that the drip line in block 3 is leaking
FormLeave form, spray record, incident report
ListTools and materials needed for planting a new bed
Short reportWhat was done today at a client's garden
Letter or emailAsking a supplier for a quote for compost

Plan the order

Put your points in a sensible order. For a report or message, use:

  • What happened or what is needed.
  • Where and when.
  • Why it matters.
  • What should be done next, and by whom.

Example plan

Reader: supervisor. Purpose: report a problem. Points: irrigation valve at the entrance lawn broken; found 07:30 Monday; water running onto the paving; I closed the main tap; need a new valve. With this plan ready, the message almost writes itself.

lessons.title: Writing clearly and checking your work
lessons.html:
Writing clearly

Tips for clear writing

  • Use short sentences. One idea in each sentence.
  • Use everyday words that the reader knows.
  • Use the correct names of plants, tools and places, for example block 3, the nursery tunnel, the front lawn.
  • Give exact facts: numbers, dates, times. Write 40 trays of seedlings, not a lot of seedlings.
  • Use paragraphs. Start a new paragraph for a new point.
  • Be polite. Use please and thank you in requests.

Example message

Monday 3 March, 07:45
To: Mr Dlamini
The irrigation valve at the entrance lawn is broken. Water was running onto the paving when I arrived at 07:30. I closed the main tap at the pump house. The lawn will not be watered until the valve is replaced. Please can we get a new 25 mm valve from the store?
Lindiwe

This message says what, where, when, what was done and what is needed. It has the date, time, the reader's name and the writer's name.

Filling in forms

  • Read the whole form first.
  • Write clearly in block letters if asked.
  • Fill in every part. Write N/A if a part does not apply.
  • Sign and date it.

Check before you hand it in

  1. Read it again as if you were the reader. Is it clear?
  2. Check the facts: names, numbers, dates.
  3. Check spelling and punctuation: capital letters, full stops, question marks.
  4. Remove words that are not needed.
  5. Ask a co-worker to read it if it is important.

Writing on a phone message or WhatsApp at work still needs to be clear and polite. Do not use slang or short forms that the reader may not understand.

Key points

  • Know your reader, your purpose and your main points before you write.
  • Put points in order: what, where, when, why, what next.
  • Use short sentences, exact facts and polite language.
  • Fill in every part of a form, then sign and date it.
  • Always read your text again and check facts and spelling.
